present.explain: A German verb's ending says who does it: ich trinke (I drink), du trinkst (you drink), er or sie trinkt (he or she drinks), wir trinken (we drink). Take the -en off the basic form and add -e, -st, -t or -en. sein (to be) and haben (to have) have forms of their own: ich bin, du bist, er ist; ich habe, du hast, er hat.
present.why: English changes its verb only for he and she (drinks); German changes it for everyone, so [[ich trinke]] and [[du trinkst]] each have their own ending.

examples.literal: I drink coffee.
You drink tea.
He drinks water.
We drink milk.

contrasts.says: English adds -s only for he, she and it; German has an ending for every person.
After will, kann or muss the second verb keeps its basic form, ending in -en: Ich will Kaffee trinken.

mistakes.why: With ich, the verb ends in -e.
With er, it ends in -t; -en is for wir.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

gern.explain: To say you like doing something, German puts gern (gladly) right after the verb: Ich trinke gern Kaffee (I like drinking coffee), Ich esse gern (I like eating). The verb is the thing you like doing; gern says you like it. Not liking it is nicht gern: Ich trinke nicht gern Kaffee.
gern.why: English uses a verb of its own, like; German keeps the verb you do and adds [[gern]]: Ich trinke [[gern]] Kaffee is I drink gladly coffee.

examples.literal: I drink gladly coffee.
I eat gladly.
My mother drinks gladly tea.
I drink not gladly milk.

contrasts.says: English says like drinking; German says drink gladly.
gern comes after the verb, which stays second: Ich trinke gern Kaffee, never Ich gern trinke Kaffee.

mistakes.why: The verb comes second; gern goes after it.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

accusative.explain: When a der word is what you have, drink, order or see, der becomes den and ein becomes einen: Ich habe den Schlüssel, Ich trinke einen Kaffee. die and das words don't change: Ich habe die Milch, Ich lese das Buch. When you order, the I'd like is left out, but the einen stays: Einen Kaffee, bitte.
accusative.why: German marks who does something and what it's done to by the little word in front: [[den]] Schlüssel is the key as the thing you have, where der Schlüssel is the key doing something itself.

examples.literal: I have the key.
I drink a coffee.
A tea, please.

examples.text: Ich habe die Milch und das Buch.
examples.means: I have the milk and the book.
examples.literal: I have the milk and the book.

contrasts.says: Only der words change: der becomes den, ein becomes einen; die and das stay.
English changes only he to him and she to her; German changes the word in front of a der noun too.

mistakes.why: Schlüssel is what you have, so der becomes den.
Kaffee is a der word you're having: einen.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: A yes-or-no question starts with the verb: Bist du fertig? (are you ready?), Trinkst du Wasser? (drink you water?). German needs no do: the verb itself goes first. After a question word like wo (where) or was (what), the verb comes next: Wo ist das Auto?, Was machen wir?
question.why: English moves a helper to the front (Do you drink water?); German moves the verb itself: [[Trinkst du]] Wasser?

examples.literal: Are you ready?
Drink you water?
Where is the car?
What do we?

contrasts.says: A statement has its verb second (Du bist fertig); a yes-or-no question has it first (Bist du fertig?).
English adds do or does; German never does.

mistakes.why: After wo, the verb comes next.
The verb keeps its du ending when it goes first.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: For this, German says dieser, and it changes with its noun the way der, die and das do: dieses Buch, diese Tasche, dieser Tisch. On its own, das points at a thing: Das ist mein Haus (that's my house), Was ist das? (what's that?). In speech, das with a noun often means that one too: Das Buch habe ich.
demonstrative.why: English has this and that; German mostly uses [[das]] for pointing, and [[dieses]] or [[diese]] when it matters which one, matching the noun like an article.

examples.literal: That is my house.
I read this book.
This bag is for you.
What is that?

contrasts.says: dieses goes with das words and diese with die words, the way das and die do.

mistakes.why: Buch is a das word: dieses.
Tasche is a die word: diese.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every German noun is a der word, a die word or a das word: der Tisch, die Milch, das Buch. The word in front follows it: ein Tisch but eine Tasche; mein Buch but meine Milch. A noun's ending is only a hint, so learn each with its der, die or das. Nouns are always written with a capital letter.
gender.why: The noun decides, and the words around it follow: [[der]] Tee, [[die]] Milch, [[das]] Wasser, though all three are drinks.

examples.literal: The tea is good.
The milk is good.

examples.text: Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone lies on the table.
Is that the table?

contrasts.says: English has one the for every noun; German has der, die or das, by the noun.
mein and meine follow the noun the same way: mein Tisch, meine Tasche.

mistakes.why: Buch is a das word: learn it as das Buch.
Milch is a die word.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

v2.explain: In a German statement the verb is always the second thing. Most sentences start with the subject (Ich lese das Buch), but anything can go first, and then the subject comes after the verb: Hier ist mein Schlüssel, Das lese ich gern, Dann gehe ich nach Hause.
v2.why: English keeps I before the verb wherever the sentence starts; German keeps the verb second, so [[Hier ist]] mein Schlüssel and [[Dann gehe ich]] nach Hause.

examples.literal: Here is my key.
That read I gladly.
Then go I home.

examples.text: Auf dem Tisch liegt ein Buch.
examples.means: There's a book on the table.
examples.literal: On the table lies a book.

contrasts.says: A yes-or-no question has the verb first instead: Bist du fertig?
English says Then I go; German says Then go I.

mistakes.why: The verb comes second, right after hier.
After dann comes the verb, then ich.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

dative.explain: After auf (on), in (in) and mit (with), for where something is or what it's with, der and das become dem and die becomes der: auf dem Tisch, in der Tasche, mit dem Auto. in dem is usually run together as im: im Auto, im Haus. Going somewhere works differently, and comes later.
dative.why: German marks where something is in the little word in front: the table is [[der]] Tisch, but on the table is auf [[dem]] Tisch.

examples.text: Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone lies on the table.

examples.text: Der Schlüssel ist in der Tasche.
examples.means: The key is in the bag.
examples.literal: The key is in the bag.
I sit in the car.
I drink tea with milk.

contrasts.says: den is for what you have or drink; dem is for where something is: Ich habe den Schlüssel, but auf dem Tisch.
English says on the table and the table alike; German changes the word in front.

mistakes.wrong: Das Handy liegt auf der Tisch.
mistakes.right: Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch.
mistakes.why: Tisch is a der word: on it, der becomes dem.
in dem Auto runs together as im Auto; it never drops.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: mein (my) goes before a der or das word, and meine before a die word: mein Schlüssel, mein Handy, meine Tasche. dein and deine (your, to someone you say du to) work the same way: dein Vater, deine Mutter. Like ein, they change with the noun's role later on: meinen, meinem, meiner.
possessive.why: my and your follow the noun, not the owner: a woman says [[mein]] Schlüssel, and a man says [[meine]] Tasche.

examples.literal: Where is my key?

examples.text: Meine Tasche liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.means: My bag is on the table.
examples.literal: My bag lies on the table.
Is that your phone?
My mother comes too.

contrasts.says: mein follows der and das words, meine die words: der Tisch, mein Tisch; die Tasche, meine Tasche.

mistakes.why: Tasche is a die word: meine.
Handy is a das word: mein.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

nicht.explain: nicht (not) usually goes near the end of the sentence, after the thing you have or drink: Ich habe das Buch nicht, Er trinkt den Tee nicht. It goes before words like fertig (ready), hier (here) and nach Hause (home): Ich bin nicht fertig, Sie kommt nicht nach Hause. Before a noun with ein, or none, German says kein instead, which comes later.
nicht.why: English puts not after a helper (I don't have); German has no helper and puts [[nicht]] after what the sentence is about: Ich habe das Buch [[nicht]].

examples.literal: I have the book not.
I am not ready.
She comes not home.
I drink not gladly coffee.

contrasts.says: English adds do or does; German has only nicht.
The verb stays second; nicht never goes in front of it: Ich habe … nicht, never Ich nicht habe.

mistakes.why: The verb stays second; nicht goes near the end.
nicht comes before fertig.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

modal.explain: After wollen (want), können (can) and müssen (have to), the other verb goes to the very end, in its basic form ending in -en: Ich will Kaffee trinken, Ich kann das Buch nicht lesen, Wir müssen noch viel machen. Only the first verb changes for who; there's no word for to.
modal.why: German closes the sentence around everything else: [[will]] … [[trinken]] holds Kaffee between them, where English says want to drink coffee.

examples.literal: I want coffee drink.

examples.text: Ich kann das Buch nicht lesen.
examples.literal: I can the book not read.

examples.means: We still have a lot to do.
examples.literal: We must still much do.

examples.means: Do you want to eat here?
examples.literal: Want you here eat?

contrasts.says: The first verb takes the form for who (will, willst, wollen); the second keeps its basic form.
English keeps the two verbs together (want to drink); German sends the second to the end.

mistakes.why: The second verb goes to the end.
After will, the basic form, ending in -en.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

formal-sie.explain: Sie, always with a capital S, is the polite you: for someone you don't know well, someone older, or anyone you'd be formal with, and to one person or more. Its verb is the same as with wir: Wissen Sie?, Wollen Sie einen Kaffee?, Gehen Sie nach Hause? du is for friends, family and children.
formal-sie.why: German splits English you in two: [[du]] for someone you know well, [[Sie]] for anyone else, and the verb follows: du weißt, [[Sie wissen]].

examples.text: Wissen Sie, wo mein Auto steht?
examples.means: Do you know where my car is?
examples.literal: Know you, where my car stands?
Want you a coffee?
This book is for you.

contrasts.says: Sie takes the -en form, as wir does: Sie wissen, Sie wollen, Sie gehen.
English has one you; German says du or Sie by who you're talking to.

mistakes.why: With Sie, the verb takes its -en form.
After für, Sie stays Sie.

source.note: Written with the German lessons, open to correction.

adjective-endings.explain: An adjective tells what something is like. After ist, offen stays offen: Eine Tür ist offen. Before Tür in zur offenen Tür, it becomes offenen. zur contains zu der, and this dative phrase takes -en on the adjective. The ending depends on the noun's gender, its case and the word before the adjective. This first example shows -en after zur; other combinations come later.
adjective-endings.why: English keeps open unchanged. German marks the adjective when it stands before the noun: zur [[offenen]] Tür.

examples.literal: A door is open.

examples.text: Ich gehe zu Fuß zur offenen Tür.
examples.means: I'm walking to the open door.
examples.literal: I go on foot to the open door.

contrasts.says: Tür is a die word.
zur means zu der; offen takes -en in this dative phrase.

mistakes.why: After zur, the adjective before Tür takes -en.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question-word.explain: wo asks where, was asks what, and wie asks how. An ordinary question starts with that word or phrase, then the finite verb: Wie kann ich helfen? With kann, the other verb still comes at the end. These are the question words met so far; more come before the question-word review.
question-word.why: English often adds do. German uses its own verb right after the question word: [[Wie kann]] ich helfen?

examples.literal: How can I help?

examples.text: Wie kann ich mit dem Essen helfen?
examples.means: How can I help with the food?
examples.literal: How can I with the food help?
How can your friend help?

contrasts.says: A yes-or-no question starts with the verb; a question-word question starts with what you ask about.
After kann, helfen keeps its basic form at the end.

mistakes.why: With ich, the modal is kann; changing the sentence into a question does not change who it agrees with.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-case.explain: Learn the object's case with the verb. helfen takes the dative: Ich helfe meinem Freund. There is no German preposition before meinem Freund, even though the case changes. In contrast, the thing you have with haben is an accusative object: Ich habe den Schlüssel. English help does not tell you which German case to use.
verb-case.why: The verb chooses its partner's case. In Ich [[helfe meinem Freund]], Freund is the person receiving help, and meinem marks the dative.

examples.text: Ich helfe meinem Freund mit dem Auto.
examples.means: I'm helping my friend with the car.
examples.literal: I help my friend with the car.

contrasts.says: Having a key uses den Schlüssel; helping a friend uses meinem Freund.
Dative forms occur with certain verbs as well as after prepositions such as mit.

mistakes.why: helfen takes the dative: meinem Freund.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.explain: To say at what time, use um, the hour, and Uhr: um zwei Uhr. Uhr stays in this form after the number. The whole phrase can stand inside a sentence or at its beginning: Mein Termin ist um zwei Uhr; Um zwei Uhr muss ich arbeiten. This card introduces whole hours only.
time-telling.why: German puts [[Uhr]] after the number, as English puts o'clock after it. [[um]] supplies at.

examples.text: Mein Termin ist um zwei Uhr.
examples.means: My appointment is at two o'clock.
examples.literal: My appointment is at two o'clock.

examples.text: Um zwei Uhr muss ich arbeiten.
examples.means: At two o'clock, I have to work.
examples.literal: At two o'clock have to I work.

contrasts.says: Um zwei Uhr is one time phrase. When it comes first in a statement, the finite verb follows the whole phrase.

mistakes.wrong: Um zwei Uhr ich muss arbeiten.
mistakes.right: Um zwei Uhr muss ich arbeiten.
mistakes.why: The whole time phrase comes first, then muss, then ich.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

purpose.explain: um … zu gives a purpose: Ich komme, um zu bezahlen (I'm coming to pay). In these examples, the one who wants the result and the one who does the action are the same: I come and I pay. Put a comma before um, and zu before the infinitive. um … zu is one way to express purpose, not the only one; a later lesson introduces another way when different people are involved.
purpose.why: English can use to pay by itself. German uses the pair [[um … zu]] to make this purpose explicit.

examples.literal: I come, in order to pay.

examples.text: Er hat kein Geld, um zu bezahlen.
examples.means: He doesn't have any money to pay with.
examples.literal: He has no money, in order to pay.

contrasts.says: Ich will bezahlen has a bare infinitive after will. Ich komme, um zu bezahlen uses um … zu for the purpose of coming.

mistakes.why: zu needs the infinitive bezahlen, not the finite form bezahlt.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

object-pronouns.explain: A pronoun changes form when a verb or preposition calls for a different case. du names the person doing something; after bei, use the dative dir: Ich bin bei dir. The English word you stays the same. This first example teaches bei dir. The later object-pronoun lesson compares the forms chosen by hearing and helping.
object-pronouns.why: Choose the form from the expression, not from English you: bei always takes the dative, so [[bei dir]].

examples.means: I want to be with you.
examples.literal: I want with you be.
I am with you.
Who is with you?

contrasts.says: bei takes the dative whether it is followed by a noun phrase or a pronoun.

mistakes.why: After bei, du must become dir.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.explain: To tell someone you address as du to call, say Ruf … an, usually with no du. The polite form keeps Sie: Rufen Sie den Arzt an, bitte. The prefix an stays at the end of the command, before a final bitte. Keep one register throughout: Ruf for du, Rufen Sie for polite you. Learn command forms with their verbs; this lesson starts with anrufen.
imperative.why: A statement says who acts; a command addresses that person directly: [[Ruf]] deinen Vater an. Polite German still names [[Sie]].

examples.text: Rufen Sie den Arzt an, bitte.
examples.literal: Call you the doctor up, please.

examples.text: Ruf deinen Vater mal kurz an.
examples.means: Give your dad a quick call.
examples.literal: Call your father just briefly up.

contrasts.says: The polite request keeps Sie; the familiar request usually leaves out du.
Both command forms put an after the object.

mistakes.right: Ruf deinen Vater mal kurz an.
mistakes.why: In this command, an splits off and comes at the end.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

particles.explain: In a friendly request, mal can make the request less abrupt: Ruf meine Mutter mal an. It does not describe a separate action and need not have a separate English word. In mal kurz, kurz supplies briefly or for a moment, while mal softens the request. The effect depends on context and tone; this lesson introduces that use of mal.
particles.why: English can soften a request with give someone a call or with the way it is said. German can add [[mal]] inside the request.

examples.text: Kannst du mal kurz den Arzt anrufen?
examples.means: Can you call the doctor real quick?
examples.literal: Can you just briefly the doctor call?

examples.text: Ruf deinen Vater mal kurz an.
examples.means: Give your dad a quick call.
examples.literal: Call your father just briefly up.
Call my mother just up.

contrasts.says: Do not translate every mal as once. Here it softens the request, while kurz supplies the short duration.

mistakes.why: mal does not change how anrufen splits: Ruf … an.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

indirect-question.explain: A question can be part of another sentence. In Ich verstehe nicht, was ich machen muss, was introduces what is not understood. That part has its own subject ich, and the finite verb muss goes last. With a modal, the infinitive comes just before it: machen muss. The surrounding sentence keeps its own order: Versteht ihr, was ich sage? begins with the verb because the whole sentence is a yes-or-no question.
indirect-question.why: German marks the embedded part with a comma and closes it with its finite verb: was ich machen [[muss]]. English keeps what I have to do.

examples.means: Do you understand what I'm saying?
examples.literal: Understand you all, what I say?

examples.text: Ich verstehe nicht, was ich machen muss.
examples.means: I don't understand what I have to do.
examples.literal: I understand not, what I do have to.

contrasts.says: In a direct question, the finite verb follows the question word. In the embedded clause, it comes last.
An embedded modal clause ends with infinitive + modal: machen muss.

mistakes.wrong: Ich verstehe nicht, was ich mache muss.
mistakes.right: Ich verstehe nicht, was ich machen muss.
mistakes.why: With muss, the other verb is the infinitive machen.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

zu-infinitive.explain: Ich habe heute viel zu tun literally says I have a lot to do today, and naturally means I'm busy today. Here zu stands before the infinitive tun. There is no um: the phrase says what there is to do, not the purpose of another action. This lesson introduces this one expression; other uses of zu with infinitives come later.
zu-infinitive.why: English uses busy for this situation. German often describes the work waiting: viel [[zu tun]].

examples.text: Hast du heute viel zu tun?
examples.literal: Have you today a lot to do?

examples.text: Ich habe heute viel zu tun.
examples.literal: I have today a lot to do.

examples.text: Mein Vater hat viel zu tun.
examples.literal: My father has a lot to do.

contrasts.says: um … zu gives a purpose. viel zu tun describes what there is to do.
After muss, the infinitive has no zu; in viel zu tun, zu belongs to this expression.

mistakes.wrong: Ich habe heute viel zu tue.
mistakes.right: Ich habe heute viel zu tun.
mistakes.why: After zu, use the infinitive tun, not tue.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

destination.explain: Going to a destination can use zu. Before a feminine noun with the definite article, zu der normally contracts to zur: Ich gehe zur offenen Tür. Going home uses the established phrase nach Hause. Here zu Fuß specifies walking. These examples do not give a rule for every kind of place; learn the destination phrase with its meaning.
destination.why: German chooses a destination phrase: [[zur]] Tür contains zu der, while [[nach Hause]] means home when going there.

examples.text: Ich gehe zu Fuß zur offenen Tür.
examples.means: I'm walking to the open door.
examples.literal: I go on foot to the open door.

examples.text: Wir gehen zu Fuß nach Hause.
examples.literal: We go on foot home.

contrasts.says: zu takes the dative even when someone is moving. zur contains the dative der.

mistakes.why: Tür is feminine: zu der Tür, normally contracted to zur Tür.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

perfect.explain: To say that someone has lost something, use a form of haben with verloren: Ich habe deinen Schlüssel verloren. Some verbs take sein instead; they come later. haben changes with the subject; verloren stays the same. In these sentences it comes at the end. In a yes-or-no question, haben goes first and verloren still comes last: Hast du den Schlüssel auch verloren? Learn verloren with verlieren; not all participles are made the same way.
perfect.why: German places the object between [[habe]] and [[verloren]]. English puts lost before your key.

examples.literal: I have your key lost.

examples.text: Hast du den Schlüssel auch verloren?
examples.means: Have you lost the key too?
examples.literal: Have you the key too lost?
We have the key lost.

contrasts.says: The finite helper is habe, hast or haben; the participle verloren does not change with the subject.

mistakes.why: The helper must agree with ich: habe.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-place.explain: In a neutral statement, German often puts a time phrase before a place or destination: Wir gehen um zwei Uhr nach Hause. English often puts that time at the end. This is a useful starting order, not a rule that makes every other order wrong. A time phrase at the beginning counts as one unit before the finite verb.
time-place.why: The sentence first says when and then where: [[um zwei Uhr]] before [[nach Hause]].

examples.text: Wir gehen um zwei Uhr nach Hause.
examples.means: We're going home at two o'clock.
examples.literal: We go at two o'clock home.

contrasts.says: A whole time phrase can come before the verb. The finite verb still comes second.

mistakes.wrong: Um zwei Uhr wir gehen nach Hause.
mistakes.right: Um zwei Uhr gehen wir nach Hause.
mistakes.why: After the initial time phrase, gehen must come before wir.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

kein.explain: kein before a noun means no, not a or not any. Geld is a das word: Ich habe kein Geld means I don't have any money. The same form appears in a question: Hast du kein Geld? The ending changes with gender and case; these first examples use the neuter accusative kein Geld.
kein.why: English often adds do not have any. German keeps haben and puts [[kein]] directly before the noun.

examples.literal: I have no money.
Have you no money?

examples.text: Er hat kein Geld, um zu bezahlen.
examples.means: He doesn't have any money to pay with.
examples.literal: He has no money, in order to pay.

contrasts.says: Use kein for no money. nicht is used for other kinds of negation, such as nicht fertig.

mistakes.why: Geld is neuter: accusative kein Geld, not keinen Geld.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

es-gibt.explain: es gibt introduces the existence or availability of something: Hier gibt es ein Sofa. The noun phrase after it is accusative: ein Sofa, but keinen Tisch. The finite verb is gibt, and es stays as its subject. For the specific location of your phone, German naturally uses ist or liegt instead; es gibt is not a mechanical replacement for every English there is.
es-gibt.why: English there is introduces a thing. German can use [[es gibt]], literally it gives, while the thing introduced is its object.

examples.literal: Here gives it a sofa.

examples.text: Gibt es vor dem Haus ein Sofa?
examples.means: Is there a sofa in front of the house?
examples.literal: Gives it in front of the house a sofa?

examples.text: Vor der Tür gibt es keinen Tisch.
examples.means: There isn't a table in front of the door.
examples.literal: In front of the door gives it no table.

contrasts.says: Tisch is masculine, so no table after es gibt is keinen Tisch.
With a place first, the order is Hier gibt es … .

mistakes.why: The finite verb gibt follows Hier.

mistakes.wrong: Vor der Tür gibt es kein Tisch.
mistakes.right: Vor der Tür gibt es keinen Tisch.
mistakes.why: The masculine object needs the accusative keinen Tisch.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 101–120, open to correction.

separable.explain: anrufen means to call someone by phone. Its prefix splits in a command: Ruf meine Mutter mal an. The polite command does the same: Rufen Sie den Arzt an, bitte. After a modal, the whole infinitive stays together: Willst du meine Mutter anrufen? This lesson compares those uses; other separable verbs come later.
separable.why: The phone-call meaning is carried by [[Ruf … an]] together. After willst, it is the single infinitive [[anrufen]].

examples.literal: Want you my mother call?

examples.text: Rufen Sie den Arzt an, bitte.
examples.literal: Call you the doctor up, please.
Call my mother just up.

contrasts.says: After willst or kannst, use the joined infinitive anrufen.
In Ruf … an and Rufen Sie … an, the prefix goes after the object.

mistakes.why: The familiar command separates an from Ruf.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 21–40, open to correction.

coordination.explain: und adds something, aber introduces a contrast, and oder offers an alternative. denn joins a reason to the clause before it. After denn, a full statement keeps its usual main-clause order: Ich bleibe im Bett, denn ich will schlafen. The finite verb will follows ich, and schlafen stays at the end. denn is especially common in writing; another way of giving reasons is more usual in everyday conversation and comes later.
coordination.why: A joining word does not always change the word order. With [[denn]], each part still has its own main-clause structure.

examples.text: Ich bleibe im Bett, denn ich will schlafen.
examples.means: I'm staying in bed because I want to sleep.
examples.literal: I stay in the bed, because I want sleep.

examples.text: Wir essen jetzt, denn wir müssen arbeiten.
examples.means: We're eating now because we have to work.
examples.literal: We eat now, because we have to work.

examples.text: Ich schlafe nicht, denn ich muss arbeiten.
examples.means: I'm not sleeping, because I have to work.
examples.literal: I sleep not, because I have to work.

contrasts.says: denn stands outside the following clause. The finite verb still follows the first constituent of that clause.
A modal remains finite, and the other verb remains an infinitive: denn ich will schlafen.

mistakes.wrong: Ich bleibe im Bett, denn ich willst schlafen.
mistakes.right: Ich bleibe im Bett, denn ich will schlafen.
mistakes.why: will must agree with ich; willst belongs with du.

mistakes.wrong: Ich bleibe im Bett, denn ich schlafen will.
mistakes.right: Ich bleibe im Bett, denn ich will schlafen.
mistakes.why: denn connects a main clause; it does not send will to the end.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 41–60, open to correction.

quantity-pronouns.explain: An amount does not always need a noun after it. Ich habe genug means I have enough: the situation supplies what there is enough of. Nimmst du auch ein bisschen? asks whether you are having a little too, without repeating the food or drink. When the noun is useful, say it: genug Wasser, ein bisschen Kaffee. These examples need no extra word meaning there.
quantity-pronouns.why: The amount can carry the meaning on its own: Ich habe [[genug]]. German does not insert a separate pronoun for the understood food or drink.

examples.means: I already have enough, thank you.
examples.literal: I have already enough, thanks.

examples.means: Are you having a little too?
examples.literal: Take you too a little bit?

examples.means: Do you already have enough water?
examples.literal: Have you already enough water?

contrasts.says: Enough and a little can stand alone in English too. The same context supplies the missing noun.
kein before a noun negates that noun phrase. These examples instead give an amount without repeating a noun.

mistakes.why: Leaving out the noun does not change the agreement: ich habe.
The finite verb still agrees with du: nimmst.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 41–60, open to correction.

two-way-prepositions.explain: For a location, in, an and auf use the dative: Das Foto steht auf dem Tisch. For the destination or new position, they use the accusative: Ich stelle das Foto auf den Tisch. The question is whether the phrase gives where something is or where it goes. Movement by itself is not the test: walking in a place can still take dative. In the lessons, an die Tür gives the new position of the sofa, while in meinem Zimmer tells where the sofa is.
two-way-prepositions.why: Compare [[auf dem Tisch]] with [[auf den Tisch]]. The article shows whether the table is the location or the destination.

examples.text: Das Foto steht auf dem Tisch.
examples.means: The photo is on the table.
examples.literal: The photo stands on the table.

examples.text: Ich stelle das Foto auf den Tisch.
examples.means: I'm putting the photo on the table.
examples.literal: I put the photo on the table.

examples.text: Wir stellen das Sofa an die Tür.
examples.means: We're putting the sofa by the door.
examples.literal: We put the sofa at the door.

examples.text: In meinem Zimmer steht ein Sofa.
examples.means: There's a couch in my room.
examples.literal: In my room stands a sofa.

contrasts.says: A place phrase can identify a location: in meinem Zimmer.
A destination or new position uses accusative with these prepositions. Other prepositions have their own rules.

mistakes.wrong: Das Foto steht auf der Tisch.
mistakes.right: Das Foto steht auf dem Tisch.
mistakes.why: Tisch is masculine; its dative article is dem, not der.

mistakes.wrong: Ich stelle das Foto auf die Tisch.
mistakes.right: Ich stelle das Foto auf den Tisch.
mistakes.why: Tisch is masculine; its accusative article is den, not die.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 41–60, open to correction.

temporal-clauses.explain: bis means until. With a time expression, it names the endpoint: bis fünf Uhr. It can also introduce a whole clause describing the event that ends the waiting or staying: Wir warten, bis du kommst. wenn introduces a clause too: a condition (if) or the time when something happens (when): Wenn du Zeit hast, trinken wir einen Kaffee. Each of these clauses has a subject and a finite verb, and the finite verb goes at the end. A comma separates it from the main clause. When the wenn-clause comes first, the main clause starts with its finite verb.
temporal-clauses.why: The endpoint or the condition can be a whole event: [[bis du kommst]], [[wenn du Zeit hast]]. The finite verb closes that clause.

examples.means: We'll wait until you get here.
examples.literal: We wait, until you come.

examples.text: Ich bleibe hier, bis du fertig bist.
examples.means: I'll stay here until you're ready.
examples.literal: I stay here, until you ready are.

examples.text: Wir warten, bis der Film anfängt.
examples.means: We'll wait until the movie starts.
examples.literal: We wait, until the movie starts.

examples.text: Wenn du Zeit hast, trinken wir einen Kaffee.
examples.means: If you have time, we'll have a coffee.
examples.literal: If you time have, drink we a coffee.

contrasts.says: bis fünf Uhr gives an endpoint with a time expression. bis du kommst gives it with a whole clause.
The prefix joins the verb in this subordinate clause: bis der Film anfängt.
A wenn-clause can come first; then the main clause starts with its finite verb: Wenn du Zeit hast, trinken wir einen Kaffee.

mistakes.why: The subordinate verb still agrees with du.

mistakes.wrong: Wir warten, bis der Film fängt an.
mistakes.right: Wir warten, bis der Film anfängt.
mistakes.why: In this bis-clause the prefix joins the verb, which goes last.

mistakes.wrong: Wenn du hast Zeit, trinken wir einen Kaffee.
mistakes.right: Wenn du Zeit hast, trinken wir einen Kaffee.
mistakes.why: In the wenn-clause the finite verb goes last.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 41–60 and widened with wenn for 81–100, open to correction.

plural.explain: A plural says there is more than one. Learn it with the noun: das Buch, die Bücher. Here u becomes ü and -er is added; other nouns form their plurals differently, so do not add -er to every noun. The plural article is die in the nominative and accusative, whatever the singular gender. In the dative, this example has den and an extra -n on the noun: in den Büchern. A plural subject also needs a plural verb: Die Bücher sind hier.
plural.why: The noun itself changes: Buch becomes [[Bücher]]. Case can add another ending, as in [[Büchern]].

examples.literal: The book is here.
The books are here.
I have two books read.

examples.text: In den Büchern geht es um die Stadt.
examples.means: The books are about the city.
examples.literal: In those books goes it about the city.

contrasts.says: Buch is neuter in the singular. Its plural uses die, just as other nouns do in nominative and accusative plural.
The dative plural in these examples is den Büchern. Learn both the article and the noun ending.

mistakes.why: A plural subject needs sind, not singular ist.
The plural article here is die, not singular das.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 41–60, open to correction.

dass.explain: dass introduces the content of a thought or statement: Ich denke, dass er zu Hause ist. The finite verb goes at the end of the dass-clause. With a modal, the infinitive comes before the finite modal: dass wir hier essen können. A separable verb stays joined: dass der Film anfängt. Put a comma before the clause.
dass.why: English can leave out that after think. German can use [[dass]] with a final verb; this is the construction practiced here.

examples.text: Ich denke, dass er zu Hause ist.
examples.literal: I think, that he at home is.

examples.text: Ich denke, dass wir hier essen können.
examples.means: I think we can eat here.
examples.literal: I think, that we here eat can.

examples.text: Denkst du, dass wir das versuchen können?
examples.means: Do you think we can try that?
examples.literal: Think you, that we that try can?

contrasts.says: The main clause still follows its own order: Ich denke. The finite verb in the dass-clause goes last.
With a modal, the lexical infinitive stands before it: essen können.

mistakes.wrong: Ich denke, dass er zu Hause bist.
mistakes.right: Ich denke, dass er zu Hause ist.
mistakes.why: The finite verb still agrees with er.

mistakes.wrong: Ich denke, dass wir hier essen kann.
mistakes.right: Ich denke, dass wir hier essen können.
mistakes.why: wir requires können, even at the end of a subordinate clause.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 41–60, open to correction.

weil.explain: weil introduces a reason and is common in everyday speech. In the standard order practiced here, its finite verb goes at the end: Ich rufe an, weil ich heute frei habe. With a modal, the infinitive comes before the finite modal. A comma separates the clauses. Verb-second clauses after weil are also heard in conversation; they are not used here as supposedly impossible wrong versions.
weil.why: Compare a reason introduced by [[denn]] with one introduced by [[weil]]. The standard weil-clause has its finite verb at the end.

examples.text: Ich rufe an, weil ich heute frei habe.
examples.means: I'm calling because I have today off.
examples.literal: I call up, because I today off have.

examples.text: Wir essen zu Hause, weil wir frei haben.
examples.means: We're eating at home because we have the day off.
examples.literal: We eat at home, because we off have.

examples.text: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich das will.
examples.means: I'm staying home because I want to.
examples.literal: I stay at home, because I that want.

contrasts.says: denn joins a reason with main-clause order. Standard weil-clauses put their finite verb last.
Both dass and standard weil-clauses have a final finite verb, but dass gives content and weil gives a reason.

mistakes.wrong: Ich rufe an, weil ich heute frei hast.
mistakes.right: Ich rufe an, weil ich heute frei habe.
mistakes.why: The finite verb must agree with ich.

mistakes.wrong: Wir essen zu Hause, weil wir frei hat.
mistakes.right: Wir essen zu Hause, weil wir frei haben.
mistakes.why: The finite verb must agree with wir.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 41–60, open to correction.

sein-perfect.explain: gehen and kommen describe a change of place and take sein in the perfect. bleiben takes sein too: Ich bin geblieben. The auxiliary agrees with the subject: ich bin, du bist, sie ist, wir sind. The participle normally closes the main clause. Do not choose sein just because an action involves movement: the verb and its use decide. The waiting in these lessons takes haben: Ich habe gewartet.
sein-perfect.why: The helper changes from haben to [[sein]], but the participle still goes at the end: Ich [[bin]] nach Hause [[gegangen]].

examples.text: Ich bin gestern nach Hause gegangen.
examples.literal: I am yesterday to home gone.

examples.text: Sie ist um drei Uhr gekommen.
examples.literal: She is at three o'clock come.

examples.text: Wir sind bei meiner Mutter geblieben.
examples.literal: We are with my mother stayed.
I have waited.

contrasts.says: The participles here use sein for gehen, kommen and bleiben, but haben for warten.
sein still agrees with the subject: ich bin, du bist, wir sind.

mistakes.why: ich takes bin.

mistakes.wrong: Wir ist bei meiner Mutter geblieben.
mistakes.right: Wir sind bei meiner Mutter geblieben.
mistakes.why: wir takes sind.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 41–60, open to correction.

reflexive.explain: In Ich habe mich gesetzt, ich and mich refer to the same person: I sat down. With du, use dich: Du hast dich gesetzt. These are reflexive uses of the accusative pronouns. setzen describes taking a seat; sitzen describes already being seated. The perfect here uses haben and gesetzt. This card covers these two people and this verb; other reflexive forms and verbs come later.
reflexive.why: German expresses sitting down with a pronoun referring back to the subject: Ich habe [[mich]] gesetzt. English simply says I sat down, without myself.

examples.text: Ich habe mich zwischen euch gesetzt.
examples.literal: I have myself between you all seated.

examples.text: Hast du dich vor die Schule gesetzt?
examples.means: Did you sit down in front of the school?
examples.literal: Have you yourself in front of the school seated?

examples.text: Ich habe mich vor das Bürogebäude gesetzt.
examples.means: I sat down in front of the office building.
examples.literal: I have myself in front of the office building seated.

contrasts.says: mich is me in an ordinary object use. Here it points back to ich and supplies the reflexive construction.
vor die Schule gives the new position. Its accusative case is separate from the reflexive mich or dich.

mistakes.wrong: Ich habe mir vor das Bürogebäude gesetzt.
mistakes.right: Ich habe mich vor das Bürogebäude gesetzt.
mistakes.why: Sitting down with setzen takes accusative mich, not dative mir.

mistakes.wrong: Hast du dir vor die Schule gesetzt?
mistakes.right: Hast du dich vor die Schule gesetzt?
mistakes.why: The person sitting down is du; the reflexive accusative form is dich.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 61–80, open to correction.

comparative.explain: früh means early. früher means earlier: it compares the time with another time, which may already be understood. In eine Minute früher, eine Minute tells how much earlier. Here the comparative describes when someone comes or goes, so it takes no extra adjective ending. This first card uses früh and früher; other comparisons and irregular forms come later.
comparative.why: The ending [[-er]] in [[früher]] adds the comparison: earlier, rather than simply early.

examples.text: Kannst du eine Minute früher kommen?
examples.means: Can you come a minute earlier?
examples.literal: Can you a minute earlier come?

examples.text: Ich bin eine Stunde früher gekommen.
examples.literal: I am an hour earlier come.

examples.text: Du kommst früh, aber ich komme früher.
examples.means: You come early, but I come earlier.
examples.literal: You come early, but I come earlier.

contrasts.says: Early becomes earlier in English; früh becomes früher in German. The other time can remain understood.
Here früher describes when. It is not an adjective placed before a noun.

mistakes.wrong: Kannst du eine Minute früher kommt?
mistakes.right: Kannst du eine Minute früher kommen?
mistakes.why: früher changes the time, not the verb construction: after kannst, use infinitive kommen.

mistakes.wrong: Du kommt früh, aber ich komme früher.
mistakes.right: Du kommst früh, aber ich komme früher.
mistakes.why: The finite verb still agrees with du.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 61–80, open to correction.

nominal-infinitive.explain: A verb can name an activity as a noun. The infinitive fahren becomes the neuter noun Fahren: das Fahren. With an article, this noun is capitalized even in the middle of a sentence: Ich finde das Fahren schwierig. As the subject, it takes a singular verb: Das Fahren ist nicht so schwierig. In Ich will fahren lernen, fahren is a verb and stays lowercase. The activity itself can be discussed without an article too, as in Fahren ist wichtig für meine Arbeit.
nominal-infinitive.why: Compare the verb [[fahren]] with the noun [[das Fahren]]. English often names an activity with -ing: driving.

examples.means: I want to learn to drive.
examples.literal: I want drive learn.
I find the driving difficult.

examples.text: Das Fahren ist nicht so schwierig.
examples.literal: The driving is not so difficult.

contrasts.says: An infinitive used as an activity noun is neuter: das Fahren.
English generally says driving without the. German can use das Fahren when discussing the activity.

mistakes.why: The activity noun is neuter; the accusative article is das.

mistakes.wrong: Das Fahren sind nicht so schwierig.
mistakes.right: Das Fahren ist nicht so schwierig.
mistakes.why: The activity noun is singular, so use ist.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 61–80, open to correction.

weak-nouns.explain: Herr belongs to the weak masculine nouns. In the singular, the subject form is Herr: Der Herr hat angerufen. The accusative object is Herrn: Ich treffe den Herrn. After mit, the dative is also Herrn: mit dem Herrn. Both the article and this noun show the case. Learn this pattern with the noun; it does not apply to every masculine noun. For example, Mann stays Mann in den Mann. This card introduces the subject, object and dative forms seen in these lessons.
weak-nouns.why: Compare der [[Herr]] with den [[Herrn]] and dem [[Herrn]]. The article is not the only word that changes.

examples.text: Hat der Herr dich schon angerufen?
examples.means: Has that gentleman called you yet?
examples.literal: Has that gentleman you already called?
I meet that gentleman today.

examples.text: Ich rede zum ersten Mal mit dem Herrn.
examples.means: I'm talking to the gentleman for the first time.
examples.literal: I talk for the first time with the gentleman.

contrasts.says: A masculine object already uses den. With Herr, the noun also changes to Herrn.
After mit, use dem Herrn. Do not add -n to all other masculine nouns.

mistakes.why: As the subject, Herr has no -n: only the other cases add it.
treffen takes the accusative: den Herrn, not the dative dem Herrn.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 61–80, open to correction.

ordinal.explain: An ordinal gives a place in a sequence. erste means first. Like an adjective, it changes its ending to fit the phrase: das erste Mal, but zum ersten Mal. In the first phrase, Mal is neuter and das already marks it. In the second, zum contains zu dem and the dative adjective takes -en. Mal here means an occasion, not clock time. The expression zum ersten Mal means for the first time. Other ordinals and dates are introduced later.
ordinal.why: The same first appears with two endings: das [[erste]] Mal and zum [[ersten]] Mal.

examples.literal: Is that the first time?

examples.text: Ich treffe sie zum ersten Mal.
examples.means: I'm meeting her for the first time.
examples.literal: I meet her for the first time.

examples.text: Ich treffe die Dame zum ersten Mal.
examples.means: I'm meeting that lady for the first time.
examples.literal: I meet that lady for the first time.

contrasts.says: The ordinal takes adjective endings: erste after das here, ersten after zum.
English keeps first unchanged. German changes the ending according to the phrase.

mistakes.why: After das in this nominative phrase, use erste.

mistakes.wrong: Ich treffe sie zum erste Mal.
mistakes.right: Ich treffe sie zum ersten Mal.
mistakes.why: zum contains the dative article dem, so the adjective is ersten.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 61–80, open to correction.

subject-pronouns.explain: The subject is the person or thing the finite verb agrees with, and its pronoun takes the subject form: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, Sie. It need not come first. In a contrast, the subject pronoun can be stressed and a repeated verb can be left out: Ihr geht, wir nicht. With sie, the verb can distinguish she from they: sie ist, sie sind. In the middle of a sentence, capitalized Sie is polite you and takes plural agreement. At the beginning, Sie has a capital for every reading, so the capital alone does not identify polite address. Use the verb and the situation.
subject-pronouns.why: English also stresses pronouns in contrasts, but sometimes chooses a different form on its own: Wer geht, du oder ich? is Who is going, you or me? German keeps the subject forms [[du]] and [[ich]].

examples.means: You guys are going, we're not.
examples.literal: You all go, we not.
Today is she here.
Today are they here.
Want you a coffee?
Who goes, you or I?

contrasts.says: ich and du are subject forms; mich and dich are object forms. The short contrast keeps the subject forms.
Polite Sie is capitalized even mid-sentence. A capital at the beginning does not distinguish polite you from she or they.

mistakes.why: The people going are the subject, so use ihr.
The alternatives answer who is going, so the subject form is ich.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 81–100, open to correction.

clause-first.explain: A clause beginning with wenn can come before the main clause. The finite verb in the wenn-clause goes at its end. The entire opening clause fills the first position of the main statement, so the main finite verb comes immediately after the comma, before its subject: Wenn du fertig bist, kannst du mich anrufen. In a command, the command form follows the comma: Wenn du Zeit hast, schick mir das Foto. Here wenn means if; it can also mean when in a time setting.
clause-first.why: English keeps you can after an opening if-clause. German treats the whole opening clause as one first-position unit and follows it with [[kannst]] [[du]]. Each clause has its own verb order.

examples.text: Wenn du fertig bist, kannst du mich anrufen.
examples.means: If you're ready, you can call me.
examples.literal: If you ready are, can you me call.

examples.text: Wenn du Zeit hast, schick mir das Foto.
examples.means: If you have time, send me the photo.
examples.literal: If you time have, send me the photo.

examples.text: Wenn das Foto fertig ist, schicke ich es dir.
examples.means: When the photo is ready, I'll send it to you.
examples.literal: When the photo ready is, send I it to you.

contrasts.says: The first position can contain a whole subordinate clause, not only a word or a short phrase.
wenn here sets a condition or time; it does not ask when something happens. An embedded question asking when uses wann.

mistakes.wrong: Wenn du fertig bist, du kannst mich anrufen.
mistakes.right: Wenn du fertig bist, kannst du mich anrufen.
mistakes.why: After the opening clause, the main finite verb comes before its subject.

mistakes.wrong: Wenn du hast Zeit, schick mir das Foto.
mistakes.right: Wenn du Zeit hast, schick mir das Foto.
mistakes.why: hast goes at the end of the opening wenn-clause.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 81–100, open to correction.

past.explain: war and hatte describe past states; musste describes a past obligation, and konnte a past ability or what someone managed to do. These simple-past forms are common in conversation. A modal still takes an infinitive: Ich musste an der Tür ziehen. The modal forms already shown include ich konnte, du konntest and wir konnten. For sein, use ich war, du warst, er/sie/es war, wir waren, ihr wart and sie waren; polite Sie also takes waren. This card covers these common verbs, not every simple-past form.
past.why: German can recount a past event with a single finite past verb. In [[Ich musste]] an der Tür ziehen, musste carries the past obligation and ziehen names the action. English uses had to pull.

examples.literal: The door was closed.
I had no key.

examples.text: Ich musste an der Tür ziehen.
examples.means: I had to pull on the door.
examples.literal: I had to on the door pull.

examples.text: Wir konnten die Tür endlich öffnen.
examples.means: We finally managed to get the door open.
examples.literal: We could the door finally open.

examples.means: Were you able to get the key out?
examples.literal: Could you the key get out?

examples.text: Du warst hier. Wir waren hier. Ihr wart hier.
examples.means: You were here. We were here. You all were here.
examples.literal: You were here. We were here. You all were here.

contrasts.says: The perfect uses a helper and participle. These simple-past examples use war, hatte or a past modal; a modal is followed by an infinitive.
The bare infinitive stays the same after a past modal: musste … ziehen.

mistakes.wrong: Ich konnte den Tür nicht öffnen.
mistakes.right: Ich konnte die Tür nicht öffnen.
mistakes.why: The past form does not change the noun phrase: Tür is feminine and takes die as the object.
The finite past modal must still occupy the second position in this statement.
After the opening damals, the finite verb waren comes next.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 101–120, open to correction.

conditional.explain: würde plus an infinitive describes something imagined, wished for or politely proposed: Ich würde gern ein Foto machen. haben and sein commonly use hätte and wäre. könnte expresses a possible ability or option; Könntest du mir helfen? is a polite request to someone addressed as du. Ich würde es nicht tun says what you would not do. An als ob clause describes an impression: Es sieht so aus, als ob sie glücklich wäre. It does not by itself establish whether she is happy. The finite verb closes that clause. These examples concern a present situation or possible action, not an unreal past.
conditional.why: English would often corresponds to [[würde]] with an infinitive. German also has single forms such as hätte and wäre. After as if, ordinary English may use is or were; the German examples use Konjunktiv II to present the comparison.

examples.text: Ich würde gern ein Foto machen.
examples.means: I'd like to take a photo.
examples.literal: I would gladly a photo make.

examples.means: I'd like to have the photo.
examples.literal: I would have gladly the photo.

examples.text: Ich wäre gern auf dem Foto.
examples.means: I'd like to be in the photo.
examples.literal: I would be gladly on the photo.
I could a photo make.

examples.text: Es sieht so aus, als ob sie glücklich wäre.
examples.means: It looks as if she's happy.
examples.literal: It looks so out, as if she happy would be.
Could you me help?

contrasts.says: konnte refers to past ability; könnte can present a hypothetical or possible ability. The umlaut changes the meaning.
Like a modal construction, würde has a finite form followed by a bare infinitive. hätte and wäre can themselves express having or being.

mistakes.wrong: Es sieht so aus, als ob sie wäre glücklich.
mistakes.right: Es sieht so aus, als ob sie glücklich wäre.
mistakes.why: wäre closes this als ob clause.

mistakes.wrong: Ich ein Foto würde gern machen.
mistakes.right: Ich würde gern ein Foto machen.
mistakes.why: The finite würde occupies the second position in this statement.
helfen takes the dative: mir, even in a polite request.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 101–120, open to correction.

future.explain: A present-tense sentence can describe a future plan when a time expression makes the time clear: Ich rufe morgen deine Mutter an. You can also use a form of werden with an infinitive at the end: Ich werde dich morgen anrufen. werden changes with the subject: ich werde, wir werden, sie wird when sie means she. With wahrscheinlich, the sentence expresses a prediction rather than certainty. The infinitive stays together, including the prefix in anrufen.
future.why: English often says will or going to where German uses a present form and [[morgen]]. With [[werde … anrufen]], German separates the finite helper from the action infinitive.

examples.text: Ich rufe morgen deine Mutter an.
examples.means: I'm going to call your mother tomorrow.
examples.literal: I call tomorrow your mother up.
I will you tomorrow call.

examples.text: Wir werden morgen wahrscheinlich zu Hause bleiben.
examples.literal: We will tomorrow probably at home stay.

examples.text: Sie wird wahrscheinlich ein Auto kaufen.
examples.means: She's probably going to buy a car.
examples.literal: She will probably a car buy.

contrasts.says: The present can refer to a future plan when the time expression or context makes that clear.
rufe … an splits in a main clause. After werde, the infinitive anrufen stays together.

mistakes.why: The finite verb werde occupies the second position.

mistakes.wrong: Sie wird wahrscheinlich einen Auto kaufen.
mistakes.right: Sie wird wahrscheinlich ein Auto kaufen.
mistakes.why: Auto is neuter: its accusative indefinite article is ein.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 101–120, open to correction.

genitive.explain: wessen means whose. It asks who a thing belongs to: Wessen Haus war das damals? Put wessen before the noun without adding an article. The form wessen stays the same with the neuter Haus and Auto and the masculine Schlüssel. In these questions, the whole phrase Wessen Haus or Wessen Schlüssel comes first, followed by war. These examples introduce the possessive question form; other genitive noun phrases come later.
genitive.why: English [[whose house]] and German [[wessen Haus]] both put the ownership question before the noun. German uses the genitive question form of wer.

examples.means: Whose house was this back then?
examples.literal: Whose house was this back then?
Whose key was that?

examples.means: Whose car was that back then?
examples.literal: Whose car was that back then?

contrasts.says: mein and dein state whose thing it is; wessen asks who owns it.
The question phrase can contain more than one word: Wessen Haus comes before war.

mistakes.wrong: Wessen das Haus war das damals?
mistakes.why: wessen goes straight before its noun, with no article after it.

source.note: Written with the German lessons 101–120, open to correction.

modal-perfect.explain: To describe seeing someone do something, German can put two infinitives after a form of haben: Ich habe den Mann schießen sehen. schießen names the action you saw; sehen names the seeing. The person seen is an accusative object: den Mann or den Polizisten. In these main clauses, the action infinitive precedes sehen at the end. In a question, the finite helper comes first: Hast du jemanden schießen sehen? This card introduces the construction with sehen; other verb groups come later.
modal-perfect.why: English says saw someone shoot or have seen someone shoot. In German, [[haben … schießen sehen]] can use sehen itself in this perfect construction, after the action infinitive.

examples.literal: Have you someone shoot see?

examples.text: Ich habe den Polizisten schießen sehen.
examples.means: I saw the police officer shoot.
examples.literal: I have the police officer shoot see.

examples.text: Wir haben den Mann schießen sehen.
examples.literal: We have the man shoot see.

contrasts.says: Ich habe den Polizisten gesehen uses the participle gesehen. With the action infinitive schießen, the examples use schießen sehen.
The person you see is an object: den Mann, den Polizisten or jemanden.

mistakes.wrong: Ich habe den Polizisten schießt sehen.
mistakes.right: Ich habe den Polizisten schießen sehen.
mistakes.why: schießen must be an infinitive in this verb group.
The person seen is accusative: jemanden.

seit-present.explain: Use seit with a starting point or elapsed time to say how long a situation has continued: Seit einem Monat schlafe ich wenig. When it still holds now, German uses the present here. A noun phrase after seit is dative: seit einem Monat, seit einer Stunde. seit gestern gives the starting point. Seit wann asks when the ongoing situation began. This also works for a repeated habit continuing over the period: Seit einem Monat wache ich früh auf.
seit-present.why: English often uses have been sleeping or have been awake. German uses the present with [[seit]]: schlafe, wache or ist. The German tense does not imply that the situation began only now.

examples.text: Seit einem Monat schlafe ich wenig.
examples.means: I haven't been sleeping much for a month now.
examples.literal: For a month sleep I little.

examples.text: Sie ist schon seit einer Stunde wach.
examples.means: She's been awake for an hour already.
examples.literal: She is already for an hour awake.

examples.text: Seit wann schläfst du so wenig?
examples.means: How long have you been sleeping so little?
examples.literal: Since when sleep you so little?

examples.text: Seit einem Monat wache ich früh auf.
examples.means: I've been waking up early for a month now.
examples.literal: For a month wake I early up.

contrasts.says: The present in these sentences describes a situation continuing now. A perfect sentence can instead recount a completed period.
A time span after seit takes the dative: einem Monat or einer Stunde.

mistakes.wrong: Seit einen Monat schlafe ich wenig.
mistakes.right: Seit einem Monat schlafe ich wenig.
mistakes.why: seit takes the dative, so use einem Monat.

mistakes.wrong: Seit einem Monat ich schlafe wenig.
mistakes.right: Seit einem Monat schlafe ich wenig.
mistakes.why: The opening time phrase occupies the first position, so schlafe comes next.

relative.explain: A relative clause identifies or describes a noun: Der Job, den ich will, ist hier. Job is masculine, so the relative pronoun belongs to the masculine set. Inside the relative clause, ich is the subject and the job is what I want, so use accusative den. With feminine Arbeit, the object form is die: die Arbeit, die ich machen möchte. The finite verb closes the relative clause. Commas mark its boundaries; when the main clause continues, close the relative clause with another comma.
relative.why: English can say the job I want without that. German keeps [[den]] in [[der Job, den ich will]]. Its case comes from its role in the relative clause, even though der Job is the subject of the main clause.

examples.text: Das ist genau der Job, den ich will.
examples.means: That's the very job I want.
examples.literal: That is exactly the job, that I want.

examples.text: Der Job, den ich will, ist hier.
examples.means: The job I want is here.
examples.literal: The job, that I want, is here.

examples.text: Das ist die Arbeit, die ich machen möchte.
examples.means: That's the work I'd like to do.
examples.literal: That is the work, that I do would like.

contrasts.says: den is required because the job is the object inside den ich will.
A relative pronoun refers back to a noun and marks its role in its own clause. dass introduces a statement without taking a noun role.

mistakes.wrong: Der Job, dem ich will, ist hier.
mistakes.right: Der Job, den ich will, ist hier.
mistakes.why: The relative pronoun is the object of will, so use accusative den.

mistakes.wrong: Der Job, die ich will, ist hier.
mistakes.right: Der Job, den ich will, ist hier.
mistakes.why: Job is masculine, so its accusative relative pronoun is den.
